cards.explanation:
Akaike Information Criterion. It solves an everyday problem: a model with
more FREE PARAMETERS — numbers the fitting procedure is allowed to choose —
always fits the data it was fitted on better, so "which fits best" has no
useful answer.

Straight line: two parameters, slope and intercept. Saturating curve: three,
because it also gets to pick where it flattens. Give the fit a third number
to tune and it cannot do worse, whether or not the extra number corresponds
to anything real.

AIC charges two points per parameter. The charge is not a convention — it is
a bias correction that makes AIC an approximately unbiased estimate of the
Kullback–Leibler distance between the true distribution and the fitted one.
Lower is better, and only DIFFERENCES between models mean anything; a single
AIC value is meaningless on its own.

How we use it: deciding whether occupancy versus signal variability is a
straight line or a saturating curve. The curve has one more parameter, so it
is guaranteed to fit better. AIC is what turns "the curve is preferred" from
a tautology into a claim.

fields.meaning: likelihood of the data under the fitted model — how well it fits
number of free parameters
the penalty — a bias correction, not an arbitrary tax

figures.caption: More parameters always fit better, so misfit alone never tells you to stop. Charging per parameter gives the total a minimum — and that is the model you keep.

cards.question: What is AIC for, and why can you not simply keep the model that fits best?
cards.reading:
Twice the negative log-likelihood of the fitted model, plus two for every
free parameter it was allowed to tune.
cards.title: AIC

cards.back:
Angle of Arrival: the direction a radio wave came from, measured at the
receiver. It needs an antenna ARRAY. The same wavefront reaches each antenna
a fraction of a wavelength apart, and that phase difference across the array
is what encodes the bearing.
cards.front: AoA — what is it, and what hardware do you need to measure one?
cards.title: AoA
cards.why:
Everyday version: hearing a car and knowing which side of the street it is
on. Two ears, one hearing it fractionally earlier. One ear gives you
loudness and no direction at all.

We do not use it. Our nodes carry two antennas and estimate a COUNT, not a
bearing. AoA belongs to the localisation half of the literature, which the
state-of-the-art chapter surveys and this system does not implement.

cards.back:
Access Point. The precise definition is more interesting than "the hub": an
AP is itself a **station**. In 802.11 a station (STA) is an addressable
destination, not necessarily at a fixed location — and a STA may be a mobile
terminal, an AP terminal, or something else again.

What makes it an AP is its ROLE. Stations group into a basic service set
(BSS); an AP connects its BSS to a **distribution system**, and several APs
on that distribution system form an extended service set (ESS) across which
a station can roam while staying in the network. A **portal** is the gateway
from the WLAN to a wired LAN.

Crucially the media are independent: how stations reach their AP and how APs
reach each other are unrelated choices.

figures.caption: An AP is a station with a job: it joins its BSS to the distribution system. Two APs on that system make an ESS, across which a station roams without leaving the network.

cards.front:
AP — define it properly in 802.11 terms. What is it, and what is it a
special case of?
cards.title: AP
cards.why:
For us the abbreviation is load-bearing NEGATIVELY. This fleet has no access
point at all. Intel firmware blocks transmit-master operation on 5 GHz for
every client card of this family, so we cannot beacon there.

We illuminate with monitor-mode injection instead — a node transmitting
frames nobody associates to, while nine nodes listen. That constraint saved
the design rather than damaging it: injection works on BOTH bands, so the
paired-band contrast survives. An AP-based illuminator could not have
produced a paired-band experiment at all.

cards.explanation:
Area Under the (ROC) Curve. A classifier does not output yes or no — it
outputs a SCORE, and somebody picks a threshold. Lower the threshold and you
catch more real positives while raising more false alarms. The ROC curve
draws that entire trade-off as one line; AUC squeezes it into one number.

The intuition worth keeping: **AUC is the probability that a randomly chosen
positive scores higher than a randomly chosen negative.** So 0.5 is not a bad
grade — it is a detector with no information whatsoever, the diagonal. 1.0 is
perfect separation.

Its virtue is being threshold-free. Two teams reporting "94% accuracy" at two
different thresholds cannot be compared; their AUCs can.

How we use it: presence detection — is anyone in the room at all. The
amplitude-variability feature does very well at that and much less well at
saying HOW MANY. One feature, two granularities, and AUC scores the easy
half.

fields.meaning: true-positive rate (recall) — of the real positives, the share found
false-positive rate — of the real negatives, the share wrongly flagged
chance a random positive outscores a random negative

figures.caption: Illustrative ROC shapes, not measured data. The diagonal is a detector that knows nothing. The further a curve bulges towards the top-left, the more real positives it catches before it starts crying wolf.

cards.question: What is AUC, what does 0.5 mean, and what is the ROC curve underneath it?
cards.reading:
The area under the curve traced by true-positive rate against false-positive
rate as the decision threshold is swept from one extreme to the other.
cards.title: AUC

cards.back:
Bluetooth Low Energy: a short-range protocol on the 2.4–2.4835 GHz band,
divided into **forty 2 MHz channels**. It shares upper protocol layers with
classic Bluetooth but its physical layer is different and not compatible.

Four ROLES, and the distinction matters. A **broadcaster** transmits only —
a one-way beacon. An **observer** receives only. A **peripheral** is simple
and holds one connection. A **central** initiates and manages several; your
phone is a central.

**Advertising** is the part we live on. A device transmits small packets on
three dedicated advertising channels — indices 37, 38 and 39 — to be seen by
anything listening. The advertisement announces presence and may carry
supported services and transmit power. Its interval is configurable from
**20 ms to about 10 seconds**.

"Low energy" is literal: short bursts of small packets, designed to run for
months or years on a small lithium battery. That is the whole trade — near
zero power, almost no throughput.

figures.caption: One advertising event: the same packet on three fixed channels, in the clear, addressed to nobody. We never connect — we listen and count. Then the radio sleeps, which is where "low energy" comes from.

cards.front:
BLE — what is it, what are the four device roles, and what exactly is an
advertisement?
cards.title: BLE
cards.why:
This is why BLE can be a calibration reference at all. We connect to
nothing, negotiate nothing, install nothing. We listen on three fixed
channels and count distinct advertisers.

Two limits follow straight from the definition. Address randomisation means
one phone can appear as several advertisers, so an identifier count exceeds a
device count. And an advertiser is not a person — the device-to-person ratio
is the weakest joint in the whole calibration spine.

Scope note: the thesis treats BLE as one INSTANCE of a device-count channel,
not the category. Ambient WiFi device activity is a second instance costing
no extra hardware, and the category is what the architecture needs.

cards.explanation:
Carrier Frequency Offset. Transmitter and receiver each run their own
crystal, and no two crystals match exactly — a few parts per million apart is
normal. Over the length of a frame that difference winds the phase around.

A metaphor that holds: two clocks disagreeing by a second a day. Either alone
looks fine; compare them across a month and the drift swamps whatever you
were timing.

CFO travels with company. Sampling-frequency and symbol-timing offsets add a
slope ACROSS subcarriers, and cyclic-shift diversity adds another rotation.
All change packet to packet, which is why raw CSI phase is unusable untreated
— signal and contamination share one measurement.

Two ways out, and we use both families. Fit the straight line across
subcarriers and subtract it, since the timing terms are linear by
construction. Or take the RATIO of two antennas on the same radio chain: both
see the same oscillator, so the offset divides out exactly, with no
estimation step at all.

fields.meaning: carrier frequency offset — the mismatch between two oscillators
the true phase of subcarrier k, the thing you want
time since the frame began
residual random rotation, different on every packet

figures.caption: Sweep the mismatch and watch the tilt grow while the SHAPE underneath never moves. That is why sanitisation works: the contamination is a straight line, so fitting a line and subtracting it leaves the room.

cards.question:
What is CFO, where does it come from, and what does it do to the phase you
measure?
cards.reading:
The measured phase is the true channel phase plus a rotation that grows with
the frequency offset and with elapsed time.
cards.title: CFO

cards.explanation:
Channel Frequency Response — how the channel treats each frequency. Indoors
the signal never arrives once. It arrives off the wall, the floor, a person,
each copy taking a slightly different time. Copies in step add; copies half a
wavelength out of step cancel. Because that offset depends on frequency, the
response ripples — strong here, in a deep null there. That is
frequency-selective fading, and the plot is what it looks like.

Everyday version: a corridor where your voice booms at one pitch and goes
dead at another. Same room, same voice, different frequency.

This is the entire case for CSI over RSSI in one picture. RSSI is that curve
collapsed to an average. A body moving through the room reshapes WHICH
frequencies null out, and the average barely moves.

The CFR has a time-domain twin, the CIR, and the two are Fourier transforms
of each other. Same channel, two views.

fields.meaning: channel frequency response — one complex number per frequency
how much the i-th path attenuated the signal
how long the i-th path took to arrive
number of paths — walls, floor, furniture, bodies

figures.caption: A second copy arriving late reinforces the first at some frequencies and cancels it at others. Averaging the channel into one number lands near the middle and erases the pattern entirely.

markers.label: a single power reading reports about this

figures.x_label: frequency across the channel (MHz from centre)

cards.question:
What is the CFR, and why does one number per channel throw away exactly what
we need?
cards.reading:
The channel at a frequency is the sum of every arriving copy of the signal,
each with its own strength and its own delay.
cards.title: CFR

cards.explanation:
Confidence Interval. The definition is exact and the everyday reading of it
is wrong. The INTERVAL is the random thing; the true value sits still. So
"there is a 95% chance the truth is in this interval" is not what was proved
— once computed, the truth is either in it or not.

The honest reading, and it is genuinely usable day to day: on Monday you
build a 95% interval for one quantity, on Tuesday for a completely unrelated
one, on Wednesday another. Keep going for a year. About 95% of all those
intervals will have trapped their true value. It is a promise about your
long-run practice, not about today's number.

The plot carries the practical consequence: width shrinks like one over the
square root of the sample. That is why "we ran a few more sessions" rarely
moves a conclusion, and why an interval that is too wide is usually a design
problem rather than an analysis problem.

How we use it: everywhere a result is reported. When a powered replication
widened the drift-trigger correlation's interval, the thesis reported the
demoted number rather than the pilot's. That is this definition being taken
seriously.

fields.meaning: the true value — FIXED, not random
the interval — RANDOM, because the data made it
the coverage, conventionally 0.95
sample size

figures.caption: Precision costs quadratically. Going from 25 sessions to 100 halves the interval — and halving it again needs 400.

cards.question:
What does a 95% confidence interval actually promise — and what does it NOT
promise?
cards.reading:
The interval computed from the sample traps the fixed true value with
probability at least one minus alpha.
cards.title: CI

cards.back:
Channel Impulse Response: the channel described in TIME rather than in
frequency. Fire one infinitely short pulse into the room; the CIR is the
train of echoes that returns — one spike per path, each at its own delay,
each with its own attenuation and phase.

The CIR and the CFR are **Fourier transforms of each other**. Same channel,
two views: a list of echoes in time, or a rippled curve across frequency.
The magnitude-squared of the CIR is the power delay profile — how much energy
arrived at each delay.

figures.caption: The echo train: the direct path first, then the wall and the floor. A richer room spreads the energy further out in delay — which is what "delay spread" names, and why wide bandwidth is needed to separate the returns at all.

cards.front: CIR — what is it, and how does it relate to the CFR?
cards.title: CIR
cards.why:
Sonar is the honest metaphor. Ping, then listen: the first return is the
direct path, later returns are the wall and the floor, and the spread between
first and last says how cluttered the room is.

Two consequences we care about. Wider bandwidth separates echoes that arrived
close together, which is why 160 MHz captures resolve structure 20 MHz
cannot. And "delay spread" — the width of that echo train — is the usual
summary of multipath richness. The thesis had an early band-contrast result
resting on delay spread; it died under re-reduction, and with it every
multipath-richness argument narrow-bandwidth hardware could have carried.

It is also what the ray tracer emits: Sionna returns a CIR per transmitter
and receiver position, and the synthetic CSI is built from it.

cards.explanation:
Cramér–Rao Bound. It answers a question engineers ask constantly and usually
cannot settle: is my estimator bad, or is this problem hard? The bound says
how much wobble is UNAVOIDABLE given what the measurement contains. Beat it
and you have made an arithmetic error, not a discovery.

Why useful rather than discouraging: it redirects effort. Near the bound, no
amount of model tuning helps — you need a better MEASUREMENT: more
bandwidth, more antennas, a longer window. Far from it, the information is
there and your estimator is leaving it on the table.

Where it bites here: we operate in a band whose primary job is carrying data,
not sensing. The integrated-sensing literature makes that a formal trade-off
— one shared waveform cannot maximise both. So the sensing fidelity available
from commodity WiFi is principled and finite, which is why "use a bigger
network" is not an answer.

fields.meaning: any unbiased estimator you might build
Fisher information — how much the data says about the quantity
that estimator's variance — its inherent wobble

figures.caption: The floor is set by the measurement, not by the algorithm. A better estimator moves the dashed line down towards the solid one and can never cross it.

curves.label: the bound — nothing goes below this

cards.question:
What does the Cramér–Rao Bound tell you, and why is that useful rather than
discouraging?
cards.reading:
No unbiased estimator can have a variance smaller than one over the Fisher
information the measurement carries.
cards.title: CRB

cards.explanation:
Every WiFi frame opens with a preamble containing symbols both ends already
know. The receiver compares what it knows was sent against what arrived,
subcarrier by subcarrier, and the ratio is the channel. It must do this
anyway or it could not decode the frame. **CSI is a by-product of ordinary
communication, and that is why sensing with it is free.**

What the values look like concretely: per frame you get a small grid of
COMPLEX numbers — one per subcarrier per antenna pair — each splitting into
an amplitude and a phase. Our adapter delivers 242 per antenna pair on a
20 MHz channel and 996 at 160 MHz. Most published CSI work runs on 56.

The useful way to picture a room: some paths bounce off things that never
move — walls, floor, shelves — and some off things that do. The static part
sets the baseline; a person walking modulates the rest. Sensing is reading
the second part while the first holds still.

A warning that follows from the definition: amplitude is relative to the
receiver's automatic gain control, so absolute values are not comparable
between captures or receivers. Anything honest is mean-scaled.

fields.meaning: the KNOWN training symbol on subcarrier k, fixed by the standard
what actually arrived on that subcarrier
the channel — a complex number, amplitude and phase
subcarrier index — tens to hundreds per frame

figures.caption: One CSI record is a column of numbers like this, tens of times a second. A body does not shift the whole curve — it changes its SHAPE.

figures.alt: A CSI amplitude waterfall: subcarrier index on the vertical axis, time along the horizontal, colour showing amplitude in decibels. Vertical streaks of darker colour cut through the field where a walking body disturbed the channel; several horizontal lines stay dark throughout, which are the nulled pilot and DC subcarriers.
figures.caption: A REAL capture, not an illustration — ten minutes from node monad05 on 5 GHz channel 48 while a person walked the room, scoped to the paced injector. Each vertical slice is one CSI record. The horizontal dark lines are structural (nulled tones); the vertical disturbances are the person.

cards.question:
What IS Channel State Information — what does the receiver measure, and what
do the numbers look like?
cards.reading:
The receiver knows what was sent and sees what arrived, so it divides one by
the other to recover the channel on every subcarrier.
cards.title: CSI

cards.explanation:
Cumulative Sum. The defect it fixes is stated plainly in the quality-control
literature: an ordinary control chart judges a process using ONLY the current
sample, ignoring its history — so it is blind to a small persistent shift,
because each reading alone looks fine.

CUSUM accumulates instead. Every reading adds its excess over a slack term to
a running total. Noise cancels because it is symmetric; a genuine shift does
not, so the total marches upward. The two knobs trade directly: a small slack
detects faster and cries wolf more often.

Everyday version: one heating bill slightly above average tells you nothing.
Twelve slightly-above-average bills in a row is a boiler problem.

How we use it: deciding when a deployed model has drifted enough to be worth
recalibrating, with the DISAGREEMENT between the CSI estimate and the
device-count reference as input. And the deployment carries a measured
warning — run purely statistically over twelve certified-empty hours, this
family of trigger fired on a third of the streams at a detected shift of a
few thousandths of a decibel. Statistically real, physically meaningless. So
the deployed trigger adds a magnitude gate: not just "did something change"
but "is the change worth a campaign".

fields.meaning: the current reading, or a residual from a predictor
the size of change you are willing to ignore
alarm threshold — larger means slower but fewer false alarms
accumulated evidence that something has shifted

figures.caption: A small step in the mean hides inside the noise of any single reading. The running total has no such problem: once the mean moves, it climbs and keeps climbing.

curves.label: the reading itself — shift barely visible

cards.question: What does CUSUM do that looking at the latest reading cannot?
cards.reading:
Keep a running total of how far readings exceed a tolerated slack; alarm when
that total crosses a threshold, then reset it to zero.
cards.title: CUSUM

cards.back:
Coefficient of Variation: standard deviation divided by mean. A spread
expressed as a FRACTION of the level rather than in absolute units, which
makes it dimensionless and comparable across things measured on different
scales.
cards.front: CV — what is it, and why divide by the mean at all?
cards.title: CV
cards.why:
Everyday version: a fifty-euro swing means one thing on a weekly shop and
nothing at all on a house price. CV is the swing relative to typical.

Two reasons we use it on CSI amplitude. The blunt one: amplitude is relative
to the receiver's automatic gain, so absolute variance is not comparable
between captures or receivers — mean-scaled is much closer to being so. The
principled one: model the channel as a fixed component plus the moving
people, and the fixed component IS the mean. Dividing by it is what the
derivation prescribes, not a convenience.

This is the workhorse feature of the thesis. When the count relation is
described as sign-stable across every environment but platform-stratified in
scale, this is the quantity being described.

cards.back:
Dynamic Frequency Selection. Parts of the 5 GHz band are **shared with
radar** — weather radar, air-traffic control, military systems. Those users
were there first, so unlicensed WiFi is admitted on one condition: listen
for radar before transmitting, and leave promptly on hearing any.

In 802.11 this is not an optional feature. DFS is one of the **MAC station
services**, listed beside authentication, data confidentiality and transmit
power control — something a compliant station does, not a setting.

Concretely: before using a DFS channel a device runs a channel-availability
check, then keeps watching while it transmits. Detect radar, and it must
vacate within seconds and stay away for a long quiet period.

figures.caption: The 5 GHz band as an experiment sees it. Channel choice is a design decision with a radar-shaped constraint attached, not a preference.
rows: Safe for long unattended runs — where our captures sit
Must listen first; can be evicted mid-session
Same, and the widest block — tempting and risky
Safe, but not available in every regulatory domain

cards.front:
DFS — what is it, what is it protecting, which channels does it cover, and
what does it do to an experiment?
cards.title: DFS
cards.why:
For an experiment the consequence is blunt: **a DFS channel can eject you
mid-capture**, through no fault of the equipment, and the gap looks exactly
like an instrument failure in the data.

That is why channel is a declared setting in every capture profile rather
than a runtime choice. Our captures sit on channel 48 — non-DFS — chosen so
a night's run cannot be interrupted by a passing weather sweep.

The honest limitation that travels with this: the WiFi channel was a FIXED
setting for the project's whole history rather than a controlled variable,
so the corpus holds no within-band channel ranking for sensing, ours
included.

cards.back:
Direct-Sequence Spread Spectrum: the original 802.11 physical layer, running
at 1 and 2 Mbps by spreading each bit across a wider band with a fixed chip
sequence. It predates OFDM and uses no subcarriers at all. It is also why
2.4 GHz has only three non-overlapping channels — spread that wide, only
three fit side by side without interfering.

figures.caption: Spreading does not add energy, it flattens it: the same power spread over more hertz, which is why a DSSS signal is robust to a narrow interferer and why only three of them fit side by side at 2.4 GHz.

cards.front:
DSSS — what is it, and why does it make a busy channel look empty in our
captures?
cards.title: DSSS
cards.why:
This is the single most important trap in reading our own data. CSI is
estimated from the OFDM preamble. A DSSS or CCK frame has no OFDM preamble,
so the radio receives it perfectly well and produces **no channel estimate
whatsoever**.

The consequence: a low CSI yield does not mean a quiet channel. It can mean a
channel full of legacy traffic the sensing path is structurally unable to
see. An empty record census and a silent room are different facts, and the
loader now reports which one it was.

cards.back:
Expected Calibration Error: whether a model's stated confidence is HONEST.
Take everything it claimed to be 70% sure about; if it was right about 70% of
those times, it is calibrated. ECE is the average size of that gap across all
confidence levels.

figures.caption: What the literature this thesis stands on actually commits to. Note the last row: there is no conventional ECE threshold to quote, and inventing one would be worse than saying so.
rows: The conformal intervals this thesis reports
Called a representative value in the risk-control literature
The convention everywhere else in the thesis
TOST requires it BEFORE the data
The corpus is silent; ECE is compared between contracts, never against a bar

cards.front: ECE — what does it measure, and how is it different from accuracy?
cards.title: ECE
cards.why:
Accuracy and calibration are independent, and the difference is operational.
A forecaster who says "70% chance of rain" and is right 70% of the time is
useful even though they are wrong three days in ten. One who says "95%" and
is right 70% of the time is worse than useless — you would carry no umbrella.

Where it earns its place: this is the metric on which the distributional
output contract separates most sharply from the point contract under
environment shift. Scored on average error alone the two look nearly
identical. Scored on whether their stated confidence survives a move to a new
room, they do not.

cards.back:
Fine Timing Measurement, standardised in IEEE 802.11. Two stations measure
the distance between them from the **round-trip time of a timestamped
exchange**.

The exchange is the whole idea. The responder sends a frame and records
exactly when it left (t1); the initiator records when it arrived (t2),
replies, and records when that left (t3); the responder records its arrival
(t4). The responder hands back t1 and t4, and the initiator computes

round-trip = (t4 − t1) − (t3 − t2)

which subtracts the far side's own turnaround. Half of that, times the speed
of light, is the distance. Roughly metre accuracy in clear line of sight,
worse in multipath.

figures.caption: Four timestamps, one subtraction. Removing the responder's own turnaround is what makes the result a distance rather than a measure of how busy the far radio was.
Why we use none of the ranging family. Each needs something from the person being measured, or from a clock we do not have.
rows: Our nodes carry no real-time clock
Two antennas — and we want a count, not a bearing

cards.front:
FTM — what is the protocol, what does each side do, and what does it need
that we do not have?
cards.title: FTM
cards.why:
Note what the protocol needs: **a cooperating peer that speaks it**, and
clocks resolving nanoseconds — light crosses a room in about ten.

The cooperation requirement is exactly the dependency this thesis avoids.
The premise is counting people who carry nothing, install nothing and do
nothing, and a person who has not opted in will never answer an FTM
request.

Even where it works it produces a POSITION. The calibration architecture
consumes counts, and a metre-grade fix for one cooperating phone is not a
headcount for a room.

cards.back:
Graph Neural Network: a network that learns over nodes and edges rather than
over a fixed grid, so its input has no required shape or ordering.

The base operation is **message passing**, and it is one line. Each node
updates itself from its neighbours:

h(v) ← f( h(v), aggregate over neighbours u of g( h(u) ) )

where the aggregate is a permutation-invariant function — a sum, a mean, a
max. That invariance is the whole trick: reorder the neighbours and the
answer does not change, so the network never learns anything about the
ordering because it cannot see one. Stack the update k times and each node
has heard from everything within k hops.

figures.caption: One message-passing step. Neighbours send transformed states, the node aggregates them with a permutation-invariant function, and updates. The invariance is what makes the model blind to layout.

nodes.label: sum, mean or max — any order gives the same answer

cards.front: GNN — what is it, and why would anyone apply one to a radio channel?
cards.title: GNN
cards.why:
The appeal for wireless sensing is exactly that. A CSI tensor's layout is
tied to one antenna and subcarrier arrangement, so a model trained on it is
shaped around that hardware — which is a large part of why swapping the NIC
breaks transfer. Encode the signal as a graph and the tie loosens, because
the model was never allowed to depend on the layout.

We do not use one. It appears in the state-of-the-art survey as one instance
of the families the field marshals against domain shift — and the same
survey cautions that machinery labelled "domain adaptation" does not by
itself establish that adaptation is what confers the transfer.

cards.back:
High Efficiency: the 802.11ax physical layer. Denser subcarrier spacing and
wider channels, designed for crowded environments with many clients rather
than for peak single-link speed.

figures.caption: What a sensing pipeline actually gets from each PHY generation. More tones is more frequency resolution, and frequency resolution is what separates multipath.
rows: What most published CSI work runs on
**Four times the tones — what our AX210 delivers**

figures.caption: The trade, stated plainly. Denser tones are not free.
rows: Four times the frequency resolution per channel
Four times the data per frame to move and store
Multipath structure narrow captures cannot separate
Results on 56 tones are not automatically results on 996
More antenna × subcarrier dimensions for the covariance
Short windows leave the covariance ill-conditioned

cards.front:
HE — what does it stand for, and what does it give sensing that older PHYs
do not?
cards.title: HE
cards.why:
For sensing the gift is RESOLUTION. Our adapter yields 242 tones per antenna
pair on a 20 MHz channel and 996 at 160 MHz. Most of the CSI literature was
written on 56.

Two things follow. More tones resolve multipath structure narrow captures
cannot separate at all. And the covariance analysis depends on the count of
antenna-by-subcarrier dimensions, so a richer tone grid changes the detection
budget directly — which means results on 56 subcarriers are not automatically
results on 996.

cards.back:
Internet of Things. The useful definition is structural rather than
aspirational: a **network of things** is built from five primitives —

- **sensors** that measure a physical property,
- **aggregators** that turn groups of raw readings into something smaller,
- **communication channels** that move data between sensing, computing and
  acting,
- **eUtilities** — the software or hardware doing the computing, a phone or
  a cloud,
- **decision triggers** — predicates that must be true before an action
  fires.

The field's surveys divide the subject three ways: **things-oriented** (the
sensors), **internet-oriented** (the middleware), and **semantic-oriented**
(making the data mean something). Their point is that IoT is useful only
where all three intersect — sensors without semantics are a data landfill.

figures.caption: The five primitives, named for this deployment. The dashed return is what makes it a loop rather than a pipeline: the trigger decides when the sensors get re-anchored.

cards.front:
IoT — give a definition with actual content, and name the parts such a
system has to have.
cards.title: IoT
cards.why:
Our deployment is one of these, part for part, and saying so precisely
beats gesturing at the word. The nodes are sensors. The capture service is
the aggregator. The tailnet is the communication channel. S3 and the
measurement lake are eUtilities. And the recalibration rule is **literally a
decision trigger** — a predicate that must hold before a campaign fires.

So the argument the thesis makes with this word is one of ORDINARINESS: the
architecture needs no bespoke hardware, only the five primitives a modern
building already has.

cards.back:
Integrated Sensing and Communication: designing one waveform, one radio and
one slice of spectrum to carry data AND perform radar-like sensing, rather
than building two systems.
cards.front: ISAC — what is the idea, and what does it cost?
cards.title: ISAC
cards.why:
It matters twice, in opposite directions.

Optimistically: it is the standardisation horizon. If access points ship
sensing as a first-class network service, CSI sensing stops being a
commodity-hardware exploit dependent on driver patches.

Pessimistically, and more usefully: ISAC theory proves a TRADE-OFF. One
waveform serving two purposes cannot maximise both — sensing accuracy is paid
for in communication rate. Operating in a band whose primary obligation is
communication, we inherit a bounded sensing budget. Attainable fidelity is
principled and finite, not something a better estimator lifts without limit.

cards.back:
Leave-One-Environment-Out: hold out an ENTIRE environment, train on the rest,
test on the one held out, and repeat for each.
cards.front:
LOEO — what is the protocol, and what question does it answer that a random
split cannot?
cards.title: LOEO
cards.why:
A random split lets windows from the same room land on both sides. The model
then learns that room's multipath fingerprint and scores brilliantly on data
it has effectively already seen. The number is real and answers the wrong
question.

Everyday version: revising with the exam paper in front of you. Your mark
says nothing about whether you could sit a different paper.

LOEO is the only honest way to ask "would this work in a building we have
never been in?", and it is the protocol behind the headline calibration
result — where two labelled anchors in the new environment recover most of
the transfer loss.

cards.back:
Line of Sight: an unobstructed straight path from transmitter to receiver.
Where one exists it usually dominates the received energy, because every
other path is longer and has bounced off something lossy.

figures.caption: Two geometries, two different features. Which one carries the count is decided by whether there is a dominant direct path to shadow.

nodes.label: strong LOS — the body BLOCKS: mean amplitude falls
no strong LOS — the body STIRS: spread rises

cards.front: LOS — what is it, and which counting feature does its presence decide?
cards.title: LOS
cards.why:
It decides WHICH amplitude feature carries the count — a real design
consequence rather than a definition.

With a strong direct path, a body standing in it blocks a large share of the
energy, so the MEAN amplitude drops: shadowing. With no strong direct path
the channel is already a diffuse mixture, and an extra body mostly stirs the
mixture, so the SPREAD rises: variance.

Two geometrically distinct mechanisms, competing rather than combining, which
is why a practical pipeline keeps both feature families and why the crossover
between them is band-dependent.

cards.back:
Leave-One-Subject-Out: hold out an entire PERSON, so the model is tested on
someone it never trained on. The same discipline as LOEO applied to identity
rather than place.
cards.front: LOSO — what is held out, and is it one of our axes?
cards.title: LOSO
cards.why:
Standard in activity recognition, where body size and gait differ enough to
be a domain shift in their own right.

NOT one of our axes. This thesis shifts on environment and on hardware, and
it counts anonymous bodies rather than recognising named ones — so subject
identity is neither a variable we control nor one we claim robustness to.

cards.back:
Medium Access Control: the layer deciding WHO TRANSMITS WHEN on a shared
medium. In 802.11 the fundamental method is CSMA/CA — a station wanting to
transmit may do so only after listening and finding the channel idle. If it
is busy, the station waits for it to clear and then waits an additional
random **backoff interval**, so that two waiting stations do not collide the
instant it frees up. The receiver acknowledges a good frame; no
acknowledgement means resend.

There is a clever shortcut: every frame announces its own length, so a
listening station can note how long the channel will be occupied and stop
physically sensing until then. That is virtual carrier sense.

"MAC address" is a separate meaning: the hardware identifier a device puts in
every frame it sends.

figures.caption: Listen, wait, wait a random extra interval, then speak. More devices in the room means more waiting — which is why our delivery deficit is an occupancy signal rather than a nuisance.

nodes.label: the random wait is what stops two waiting stations colliding

cards.front:
MAC — what does the layer actually do, and how does that become an occupancy
signal?
cards.title: MAC
cards.why:
Both halves are load-bearing, in different chapters.

The protocol half gives us a count channel for free. More active devices
means more competing traffic, which means our paced probe defers more often
and lands less reliably. That delivery deficit rises with activity — an
occupancy signal already recorded in every capture ever taken.

The address half is the privacy floor. Phones randomise their MAC address
precisely so they cannot be tracked, so one phone can appear as several
identifiers. Counting identifiers overcounts devices — before you even reach
the harder question of devices versus people.

cards.back:
Mean Absolute Error: average the size of each mistake, ignoring direction. In
our units it reads directly — "on average, off by about one person".
cards.front: MAE — what is it, and why does this thesis refuse to report it alone?
cards.title: MAE
cards.why:
It is kept for two good reasons: the literature reports it so comparison
needs it, and a distribution's mean must not be allowed to drift unnoticed.

It is refused as the ONLY metric for an empirical reason rather than a
stylistic one. Scored on average error alone, the point and distributional
output contracts are nearly indistinguishable under environment shift. Scored
on where they place their probability mass, and on whether their stated
confidence stays honest, they are not remotely so — and it is the second pair
that predicts whether a deployment moved to a new room can be trusted.

Reporting only average error would have concealed the single clearest
cross-environment result the thesis holds. That is the argument, and it is
worth being able to make.

cards.back:
Multiple-Input Multiple-Output: several antennas at each end, so several
spatially distinct copies of the channel exist at once. In communication it
buys throughput and robustness; in sensing it buys viewpoints.
cards.front: MIMO — what is it, and what does it change about a CSI record?
cards.title: MIMO
cards.why:
It turns CSI from a vector into a TENSOR — one channel value per
transmit-and-receive antenna pair, per subcarrier, per frame. Each pair sees
the room from a slightly different vantage, so a body affects them
differently.

Two practical consequences. The CSI-ratio trick exists only because two
antennas share one radio chain and therefore share its oscillator errors
exactly. And the covariance analysis counts antenna-by-subcarrier dimensions
as one number, so antennas and subcarriers trade against each other in
setting how many occupants are detectable at all.

cards.back:
Network Interface Card: the radio itself — chipset, firmware, antennas, and
the driver exposing them.
cards.front:
NIC — why is a piece of hardware terminology one of this thesis's central
findings?
cards.title: NIC
cards.why:
Because swapping it breaks a trained counter MORE than swapping the room
does, and that ordering was not the expected one.

The mechanism: every environment shows the same RANK relation — more people,
more variability — so presence detection transfers cold. But two hardware
platforms sit in cleanly separated variability bands, so the ABSOLUTE mapping
from signal to count is device-specific. Hold the platform and change the
room: small penalty. Hold the room and change the platform: a penalty of a
couple of persons.

This is the empirical reason calibration must be per DEVICE, not merely per
room, and why the thesis says hardware independence stops at the feature
interface. It also answers device heterogeneity, which the recent
generalisability survey ranks first among domain-shift factors.

cards.back:
Non-Line of Sight: no unobstructed path, so everything arriving has bounced,
diffracted, or passed through something.
cards.front: NLOS — what is it, and why is it not simply "worse"?
cards.title: NLOS
cards.why:
For RANGING it is unambiguously worse: every extra bounce adds path length,
so a distance inferred from strength or delay reads too far. That is much of
why BLE trilateration errors indoors are measured in metres.

For device-free SENSING it is not a defect but a regime. A diffuse channel is
a mixture of many comparable paths, so a body perturbs many at once — and the
variability feature does well precisely there.

Same physics, opposite verdicts, which is one reason the two modalities in
this thesis fail in disjoint ways.

cards.back:
Node–Relation Graph: IndoorGML's dual-space view of a building. Primal space
is the rooms themselves; the dual is a graph with a node per room and an edge
wherever two rooms connect. It is what routing runs on.
cards.front: NRG — what is it, and what did we learn it does NOT predict?
cards.title: NRG
cards.why:
It is a natural thing to reach for when asking what makes a floor easy or
hard to sense — and this thesis tested that and found it does NOT.

Room adjacency correlates with coverage only through what it travels with:
floor area, and how many receivers were placed. Hold those fixed and the
topology signal disappears. What drives recoverability is receiver DENSITY
and placement.

The hypothesis was superseded rather than merely refuted: the question
survived, the variable was wrong.

cards.explanation:
Orthogonal Frequency-Division Multiplexing. Rather than send one fast stream
over a wide channel, split the channel into many narrow subchannels and send
many slow streams in parallel.

Why bother: a wide fast signal meets a channel that treats different
frequencies differently, and untangling that is hard. Each narrow subchannel
is small enough that the channel looks FLAT across it — one complex number
describes it completely, so equalisation becomes a division rather than a
deconvolution.

"Orthogonal" is the trick that makes it cheap. Subcarriers are spaced so that
each one's spectrum is exactly zero at every other one's centre: they overlap
heavily and still do not interfere. In practice it is an inverse FFT at the
transmitter and an FFT at the receiver, with a guard interval between symbols
so echoes of the previous symbol die out first.

Two consequences for us. Those per-subchannel complex numbers ARE the CSI —
no OFDM, no CSI. And the tone axis is a grid, not a ruler: some subcarriers
are pilots and the centre one is nulled, so subcarrier index does not map
linearly onto frequency, and a plot that pretends otherwise is lying.

cards.question: What does OFDM do, and what does "orthogonal" actually mean here?
cards.reading:
Each subcarrier's spectrum is a sinc centred on its own frequency, and its
zeros land exactly on every other subcarrier's centre.
cards.title: OFDM

cards.back:
Physical Layer: where bits become radio — modulation, coding, timing, and the
channel estimation a receiver performs to decode a frame. Notably, 802.11
standardises ONLY the two lowest layers, physical and data link; everything
above is common to all IEEE LANs and does not know whether the medium is
wireless.

figures.caption: Everything above the link layer is the same whether the medium is radio or copper. CSI exists only at the bottom — and whether you may read it is a decision the chipset vendor makes, not the standard.

cards.front: PHY — what is it, where does 802.11 stop, and what does the vendor control?
cards.title: PHY
cards.why:
It is where our observable is born and where somebody else decides whether we
may read it. CSI is computed in the PHY as a normal step of demodulation and
then usually discarded; getting at it needs patched firmware or a driver that
chooses to expose it.

That is a structural limitation of the modality, not a local inconvenience:
modern chipsets increasingly restrict raw CSI access, narrowing the hardware
anyone can build on. The 802.11bf amendment is the field's answer —
standardise the measurement so it stops depending on vendor goodwill.

cards.back:
Physics-Informed Neural Network: train on data as usual, but add a second
loss term penalising violation of a known physical law. The network is
rewarded for predictions that fit the data AND obey the physics.
cards.front: PINN — what is the construction, and what happened when we tried it?
cards.title: PINN
cards.why:
The appeal is obvious where labels are scarce: physics is free supervision,
and it demonstrably works in traffic-state estimation.

We tested it on indoor crowd density with the mass-conservation law and it
FAILED — in a way more informative than a plain null. Swapping the physics
for a constant version, then for an ANTI-PHYSICAL version, changed the result
not at all, while plain smoothing with no conservation content beat every
variant. A term whose benefit survives inverting the law it encodes is not
acting as physics.

Reported as a documented negative, because the idea is attractive enough that
it will be proposed again and the evidence retiring it is exactly
reproducible.

cards.back:
Root-Mean-Square Error: square each mistake, average, take the root. The
squaring punishes large mistakes disproportionately, so it is dominated by
the worst cases in a way average absolute error is not.
cards.front: RMSE — how does it differ from MAE in practice?
cards.title: RMSE
cards.why:
Choosing between them states what you fear. If being badly wrong occasionally
is much worse than being slightly wrong often — an evacuation estimate, say —
the squared metric matches your preference. If all mistakes cost in
proportion, average absolute error does.

Where it appears here: the density-estimation ablation that retired the
physics prior. The matched, constant and anti-physical closures landed on the
same high-density value, and that is the observation which settled it.

cards.back:
Ranked Probability Score: scores a whole predicted DISTRIBUTION over ordered
categories, rewarding probability mass placed near the truth. Because the
bands are ordered, being one band out is penalised less than being three out
— which plain classification accuracy cannot express at all.
cards.front: RPS — what does it score that accuracy cannot?
cards.title: RPS
cards.why:
Everyday version: forecasting tomorrow's temperature band. Guessing 15–20°C
when it is 21°C is a near miss; guessing 0–5°C is not. Accuracy calls both
simply wrong.

It is the metric on which this thesis's two output contracts separate. Under
environment shift the point contract degrades markedly on band RPS while the
distributional contract does not move at all — with feature, corpus and
splits held fixed so that only the contract varies. That design is what makes
the result hard to attack: nobody can say the distributional model was simply
a better model.

cards.back:
Received Signal Strength Indicator: one number per received frame, the total
power that arrived. No frequency detail, no phase, no per-path structure —
the CFR curve collapsed to its average.
cards.front: RSSI — what is it, and why is it both too coarse and good enough?
cards.title: RSSI
cards.why:
Both verdicts are true at once, and holding both is the point.

Too coarse for body-scale sensing: a person changes WHICH frequencies fade,
and averaging is exactly the operation that erases that. This is the
one-sentence case for CSI.

Good enough as a zone anchor: for BLE we only need to know roughly how far an
advertiser is, and a coarse bracket does that. The thesis treats BLE RSSI as
a range BRACKET — enough to associate an advertisement with a zone — never as
a ranging signal. Multipath swings it by tens of decibels over small
displacements, and a body absorbs several more depending on which pocket the
phone is in.

cards.back:
Round-Trip Time: send, wait for the reply, halve the elapsed time, multiply
by the speed of light. It avoids needing synchronised clocks, because only
one clock measures the interval.
cards.front: RTT — what is it, and what is the catch indoors?
cards.title: RTT
cards.why:
The catch is scale. Light crosses a room in a few nanoseconds, so metre
accuracy needs nanosecond timing, and any processing delay at the far end
must be known and subtracted exactly.

It also needs a cooperating peer — the same dependency FTM has, and the same
reason we use neither. Surveyed as an alternative primitive, not implemented.

cards.back:
Receiver. In our deployment, nine of the ten nodes: monitor-mode listeners
extracting CSI from frames they were never meant to receive.
cards.front: RX — and why does it matter that we have nine of them rather than one?
cards.title: RX
cards.why:
The count is the contribution. A single monitor cannot see that two receivers
hearing the SAME transmitter on the SAME channel at the same moment disagree
— and ours disagree by around a dozen points of delivered fraction.

That spread is invisible to any single-monitor methodology, and no corpus
paper reports it because none operates an array that could. It matters
practically too: the remedy the literature prescribes for irregular sampling
was formed on single monitors at far lower rates, and whether it survives this
spread is an open question this instrument can actually answer.

cards.back:
Sampling Frequency Offset: the receiver's converter ticks at a slightly
different rate from the transmitter's, so samples are taken fractionally
early or late and the error compounds across the frame.
cards.front: SFO — what is it, and what shape does it leave in the data?
cards.title: SFO
cards.why:
The useful fact is the SHAPE it produces: a phase error growing LINEARLY with
subcarrier index. That linearity is no coincidence — it follows from a timing
error being a frequency-domain slope.

And it is what makes sanitisation tractable. Unwrap the phase across
subcarriers, fit a straight line, subtract it. You have removed the
instrument and kept the room, without ever knowing the offset itself.

cards.back:
System on Chip: processor, memory controller and peripherals on one die —
what a Raspberry Pi is built around.
cards.front: SoC — why does a packaging term appear in a measurement chapter?
cards.title: SoC
cards.why:
Because its TEMPERATURE turned out to be a covariate of the measurement.
Across a twelve-hour run the per-node phase-drift slope ordered perfectly
with mean die temperature on passively cooled nodes.

Reported carefully: with five nodes the observed significance sits at the
attainable floor and the result turns on a fraction of a degree, so it is a
strong monotone TREND and a lead, not an established effect. It is worth
reporting because it suggests amplitude drift and phase drift have different
causes — one environmental, one thermal — which is a candidate separation for
the recalibration trigger.

Practical corollary: the fan splits the fleet into two thermal populations,
and a node can be silently throttled while every governor reading looks
healthy.

cards.back:
Symmetric Positive Definite: the class covariance matrices belong to. They do
not live in flat space — the set of them is a curved manifold, so averaging
two covariance matrices entry by entry gives a geometrically wrong answer.
cards.front: SPD — what is it, and where did it show up here?
cards.title: SPD
cards.why:
That curvature is why a whole family of methods exists to move covariance
matrices between domains ALONG the manifold rather than through the
straight-line middle.

We ran one, as one of four mathematically independent LABEL-FREE alternatives
tested under pre-registered kill lines. It recovered only a small share of
the cross-environment gap and lost to a plain scalar recalibration fitted on
two labelled anchors. Reported as run and lost, not omitted — that is what a
kill line is for.

cards.back:
Symbol Timing Offset: the receiver opens its FFT window slightly early or late
relative to the true symbol boundary. Because a time shift is a
frequency-domain phase ramp, the effect is again a slope across subcarriers.
cards.front: STO — what goes wrong, and what does it share with SFO?
cards.title: STO
cards.why:
It shares its SHAPE with sampling-frequency offset, which is convenient: one
line fit removes both. It is also why phase is treated as guilty until proven
innocent in CSI work while amplitude needs far less repair.

Together with carrier-frequency offset and cyclic-shift diversity these terms
vary packet to packet, so no fixed correction exists — sanitisation is an
estimation problem on every frame.

cards.back:
Time of Arrival: absolute travel time from transmitter to receiver. Unlike
round-trip timing it is one-way, so it needs both ends to agree on the time
to within nanoseconds.
cards.front: ToA — what does it need that we do not have?
cards.title: ToA
cards.why:
Our nodes cannot. They carry no real-time clock, so a node boots believing it
is some time in the past, and the time daemon may STEP the clock in the
middle of a session.

We discipline against one node of the fleet rather than a public source,
because the science needs relative coherence between observers more than
correct absolute time. That is a deliberate choice with a consequence every
reduction must respect: bin on each record's OWN timestamp, never on when the
session started, or a clock seam appears as a physical event.

cards.back:
Time of Flight: the propagation time itself. Time of Arrival is WHEN the
signal landed; time of flight is HOW LONG it took. In practice the terms are
used almost interchangeably, and both name the distance-from-delay primitive.
cards.front: ToF — same as ToA?
cards.title: ToF
cards.why:
Worth knowing mainly so two words for one idea do not catch you out. Neither
is used here — we estimate how many, not where, and the fleet's clock
arrangement rules out one-way timing regardless.

cards.back:
Two One-Sided Tests, the standard equivalence test. It asks "are these two
things close enough to be treated as the same?" by testing separately that
the difference is not meaningfully above, and not meaningfully below, a
margin declared in advance.
cards.front: TOST — what question does it ask, and why can a plain test not ask it?
cards.title: TOST
cards.why:
An ordinary significance test can only FAIL to find a difference, and failing
to find one is not evidence there is none — it might just mean too little
data. Equivalence testing inverts the burden of proof, which is the only
honest way to claim two methods perform the same.

Where it bites, and it bites us: the drift-triggered recalibration rule
FAILED an accuracy-equivalence test against a fixed schedule. So the thesis
does not claim parity. It claims what it can prove — the trigger spends
roughly half the calibration budget at a small accuracy cost, which is a cost
frontier rather than a free lunch.

Declaring the margin BEFORE seeing the data is what makes the answer binding.

cards.back:
Transmitter. One node of the ten, running as a paced illuminator: it emits
frames at a commanded rate that nobody associates to and nobody replies to.
cards.front: TX — and what changes when you own it?
cards.title: TX
cards.why:
Owning the transmitter is what turns a deployment into an EXPERIMENT. It
fixes channel, band, modulation and rate, so the stimulus is a controlled
variable rather than whatever the building happened to send.

It also creates the reference that makes impairments measurable. Because we
know exactly how many frames were commanded, we can say what fraction
arrived — which is how delivery became a measurand rather than an assumption,
and how the rate ladder could show that delivery tracks competing channel
load rather than commanded rate.

cards.back:
The IEEE 802.11 family of wireless LAN standards. A certification brand
rather than a technology name, but universally used as one. It operates on
unlicensed spectrum around 2.4 GHz and between 5 and 5.8 GHz.
cards.front: WiFi — what is the deployment argument, stated without enthusiasm?
cards.title: WiFi
cards.why:
The argument for building on it is NOT that it senses well. Dedicated radar
senses better; cameras see more. The argument is twofold and narrow: it is
already in the building, and the channel estimate the sensing depends on is
already being computed for communication.

Marginal cost near zero, and no new device in anyone's room. That is the
whole deployment case, and overstating it is a defense trap — the honest
version concedes a purpose-built sensor would outperform this, and argues
cost and ubiquity instead.

cards.back:
Wireless Local Area Network: the scope 802.11 standardises. The 802.11bf
amendment adds a WLAN SENSING procedure — negotiation frames, defined
measurement instances, and a reporting format — so a compliant access point
can be ASKED for channel measurements alongside normal traffic.
cards.front: WLAN — what does 802.11bf add to it, and what is its status?
cards.title: WLAN
cards.why:
It matters because it would make sensing hardware-agnostic. Today CSI access
depends on patched firmware and reverse-engineered drivers, and every dataset
is bound to the chipset that produced it — which is the root of the field's
reproducibility problem.

Status has to be stated honestly: the amendment is in final ratification and
early commercialisation, so interoperable CSI sensing is a PROSPECTIVE
capability. Our experimental work runs on pre-standard commodity hardware and
the thesis says so.

choices: Access Point — yes, the fleet runs dual-band APs on 2.4 and 5 GHz.
Access Point — but the fleet has none. Intel firmware blocks 5 GHz transmit-master, so illumination is monitor-mode injection on both bands.
Access Point — the fleet runs 5 GHz APs only, since 2.4 GHz is too congested.
Access Point — the phones act as the APs during a session.
cards.explanation:
There is no access point in this deployment, and the reason is a vendor
constraint rather than a preference: Intel's regulatory mechanism blocks
transmit-master on 5 GHz for every client card of this family, and forcing it
past the kernel crashes the CSI backport. Monitor-mode injection works on
BOTH bands, which restores the paired-band contrast an access-point
illuminator would have foreclosed. The first option is the answer a reader of
an early draft would give; the fourth confuses the participant instrument,
which is a paced emitter and a label source, with an access point.
cards.question:
A committee member asks what AP stands for and whether your access points are
dual-band. What is the correct answer?
cards.title: The trap in the list

cards.back:
Wi-Fi CSI can count people, but every deployed model decays: the
count→signal mechanism is universal (positive rank correlation in 7/7
real environments), while the absolute mapping is environment- and
hardware-specific and drifts. My contribution is (1) a four-pillar formal
theory explaining and predicting this — partial-pooling calibration,
a derived concave scattering law, state-space fusion, spectral counting +
submodular placement; (2) a BLE-calibrated architecture where cheap
continuous BLE monitoring triggers periodic recalibration campaigns;
(3) an evidence programme — reproducible campaigns, real-data
validations, a pre-registered hardware protocol, and a deployed Pi5/AX210
capture fleet.
cards.front: "Summarise your contribution in two minutes."
cards.title: The elevator pitch

cards.back:
Occupancy is the master variable for building energy, safety, and space
operations, and cameras fail exactly where deployment happens: privacy
law and acceptance, lighting, occlusion, cost of coverage. RF sensing
reuses existing infrastructure and counts WITHOUT identifying. The open
problem is not detection — it is keeping calibrated accuracy over months
without labelled data, which is precisely what the thesis addresses.
cards.front: "Why is crowd counting worth a doctorate? Cameras exist."
cards.title: Why does this matter

cards.back:
BLE is already carried by occupants and installed as infrastructure; it
gives a coarse count without identity; narrowband RSSI at many anchors is
measurably better at location fingerprinting than sparse wideband CSI
links (2.49×); and it drifts DIFFERENTLY from CSI, which is what makes
the cross-modal disagreement statistic informative. Its sufficiency as
ground truth is itself a stated, gated hypothesis — not an assumption.
cards.front: "Why BLE as the calibration side-channel and not another sensor?"
cards.title: Why BLE

cards.back:
Real-data accuracy claims currently ride on public datasets, so
cross-dataset confounds remain until first-party capture closes the
loop; the flagship calibration hypothesis is still plausible, not
supported — no public dataset has synchronized BLE + CSI + counts, which
is exactly why the IP-106 protocol and the AX210 fleet exist. I state
this before the committee does.
cards.front: "What is the biggest threat to the validity of your results?"
cards.title: Biggest weakness

cards.back:
Each hypothesis carries an explicit defeater and gate. Flagship: if the
IP-106 multi-week two-site study shows periodic BLE recalibration does
not outperform one-shot calibration (or BLE-vs-headcount R² < 0.7, so
the ground truth itself fails), the architecture claim falls. The
portfolio already contains executed refutations — continuity prior,
topology fingerprint — showing the machinery falsifies for real.
cards.front: "What result would falsify your central claim?"
cards.title: What would change your mind

cards.back:
Three things: (1) the calibration plane is FORMALISED — partial pooling
with platform nesting, where the measured 42% two-anchor recovery is
reproduced as empirical-Bayes shrinkage, and placement becomes
Bayesian-optimal design; (2) the trigger is cross-MODAL — an independent
cheap modality detects drift where self-monitoring provably false-alarms
(17%); (3) the economics are stated honestly as condition-based
maintenance: parity at ¼ spend, not accuracy magic. Novelty is anchored
per-hypothesis against named prior art in the frontmatter.
cards.front: "Recalibration for drifting sensors is old news. What is new?"
cards.title: Novelty interrogation

cards.back:
Because transfer is the problem, not fit: learned fingerprints break
under layout change (feature-type result, ratio 0.076) and synthetic
training data over-codes environment (0.99 vs 0.83, unclosable by
impairments). A physically derived low-dimensional observable —
amplitude variance with a concave law — travels across 7 environments
and stays interpretable enough to calibrate with 2 anchors. Deep models
can sit on top later; the calibration theory is what makes ANY estimator
deployable.
cards.front: "Why calibrated classical features instead of end-to-end deep learning?"
cards.title: Deep-learning challenge

cards.back:
Real: 7-env LOEO (0.72/1.32/1.75/2.07 ladder, 42%), OPERAnet MI 0.174
in-band, WiMANS dual-band re-analysis (0.71/0.28), scattering-law fits
(5/7, 3/3), first AX210 link measurements. In-silico: filter numbers
(0.53, ρ 0.97), material-drift 74%, observability paradox, anchor-
placement recovery, all fingerprint ladders. I keep the two lists
separate in every chapter — sim informs structure, real data carries
accuracy.
cards.front:
"Which of your numbers would you defend as REAL evidence, and which are
simulation?"
cards.title: Sim/real division

cards.back:
The architecture is designed for estates: hierarchical calibration
shares statistical strength across zones (new zones start at the nested
prior, 1.49 not 1.97); the trigger allocates a fixed calibration budget
to the zones that drift (¼-spend parity measured on a 4-zone estate);
placement is submodular so greedy planning is near-optimal per floor.
Saturation is the physical limit — the concave law says marginal count
information vanishes in dense hubs, so I claim counting bands, not
unbounded N.
cards.front: "Does this scale beyond one room — a mall, a campus?"
cards.title: Scaling question

cards.back:
The design goal is count-without-identify: CSI features are aggregate
channel statistics, not tracks or identities; BLE is used for coarse
presence counts, not device-level trajectories, and the ground-truth
protocol runs under institutional consent in staged spaces. RF counting
is the privacy-PRESERVING alternative to cameras (rusca2024), and
802.11bf standardisation is bringing exactly this sensing into every AP
— better to build its calibration theory with privacy as a constraint.
cards.front: "You are sensing people who did not consent. Ethics?"
cards.title: Privacy and ethics

cards.back:
Because the calibration hypotheses need synchronized BLE + CSI + counts
over weeks — no public dataset has it. Commodity extraction stacks were
x86/legacy-NIC bound; the AX210-on-Pi5 port plus our csid daemon gives a
14-node, thermally characterised, remotely operated fleet with a
self-describing capture format — and building it surfaced silent bugs
(chain-major layout, imag-first I/Q) that would have corrupted every
phase analysis downstream.
cards.front: "Why build your own capture hardware instead of using existing tools?"
cards.title: Why a fleet

cards.back:
The hardware evidence legs: IP-106 staged-room captures (calibration
regimes, drift horizons), the seated-crowd spectral leg, and the
low-density phasor-scaling leg — each pre-registered with locked
analyses. Theory and writing are ahead of the data: four pillars are
threaded through the chapters, two already real-data supported. The
thesis stands on the theory + existing real validations; the fleet turns
supported into strong.
cards.front: "What remains between today and a defended thesis?"
cards.title: Timeline

cards.back:
A SELF-LABELLING reference: an independent source of occupancy ground truth
that can re-anchor the estimator when its environment changes, without an
engineer collecting labels.
cards.front:
In one sentence, what does CSI counting most need that it cannot supply
itself?
cards.title: Why CSI needs a partner at all
cards.why:
The CSI chapter established the need structurally — environmental
sensitivity, hardware heterogeneity, multi-person ambiguity — and
deliberately left the case for BLE to be earned here rather than assumed
there.

cards.back:
The log-distance path-loss model: received level falls as ten times the
path-loss exponent times the log of distance over a reference distance,
plus a zero-mean Gaussian shadowing term. The exponent n is the
per-environment parameter.
cards.front:
Write the model behind BLE ranging and name the parameter that must be
calibrated per environment.
cards.title: The range primitive
cards.why:
It is not universal. Fitted exponents run from 2 in free space to above 4
in cluttered indoor spaces, varying with building materials, furniture and
obstruction. Anyone quoting a single indoor exponent is quoting one
building.

choices: Because BLE advertises on three channels and they have different transmit powers.
Because the actual received power is the superposition of numerous reflected, diffracted and shadowed components, while the path-loss model assumes only distance-dependent mean attenuation.
Because address randomisation prevents associating consecutive readings with one device.
Because the receiver's automatic gain control has not settled.
cards.explanation:
Multipath causes rapid fluctuation across small displacements, potentially
spanning tens of decibels, and human bodies at 2.4 GHz add attenuation
varying with posture and orientation. The model assumes a mean; the
measurement is a superposition. Without statistical correction — temporal
averaging, filtering, or weighted least-squares that down-weights
high-variance measurements — raw multilateration yields errors of several
metres. Randomisation is a real problem in this chapter, but it bounds
identifier-to-device counting, not ranging.
cards.question: Why is one instantaneous BLE RSSI reading a poor proxy for distance?
cards.title: Why a single reading is useless

cards.back:
A metre-grade BLE position may GATE which link's sensitive region a body
occupies. It can NEVER predict per-zone phase.
cards.front: The thesis bounds what a BLE position can be used for. State the bound.
cards.title: What BLE position is allowed to be used for
cards.why:
The bound comes from the thesis's own Fresnel-geometry analysis, not from
caution. It is what keeps the positional leg of the campaign honest: the
census leg is the load-bearing one, because the calibration architecture
consumes COUNTS, not positions.

cards.back:
It bounds how well an IDENTIFIER count approximates a DEVICE count — one
phone rotating its address becomes several pseudonyms, inflating the tally.
cards.front: What does MAC-address randomisation bound, and what does it NOT bound?
cards.title: The privacy floor
cards.why:
It says nothing about the larger and more awkward gap: a device count is
not a headcount at all. Keeping those two conversions separate — identifier
to device, device to person — is what stops a single fudge factor from
absorbing both.

choices: Because the published figures come from offices rather than libraries.

Two objections: the factor is not stationary — it varies by hour, by day, and more sharply across crowd TYPES — and a point correction converts an unknown bias into a confident number, moving the estimate without widening it.
Because the conversion is not identifiable from a device count alone.
Because randomisation already inflates the identifier count by a similar factor, so the two cancel.
cards.explanation:
The second objection is the more basic one, and it is the one that connects
to the output contract. Moving an estimate without widening it is precisely
the wrong response to not knowing something. A commuter flow, a lecture
cohort and an exam hall differ in carriage in ways no single scalar spans —
so importing one is not conservative, it is confidently wrong in an unknown
direction.
cards.question:
Camera-labelled building studies report device-to-occupant ratios near 1.2.
Why does the thesis refuse to just multiply by one?
cards.title: The rejected remedy

cards.back:
Two observations of ONE occupancy state with DISJOINT NUISANCE STRUCTURES
determine both the count and the device-to-person ratio, where either alone
leaves them confounded.
cards.front:
State the identification argument in one sentence, and name the property
that makes it work.
cards.title: The joint identification argument
cards.why:
Disjointness is the property. CSI perturbation responds to bodies,
device-free, indifferent to what those bodies carry; device activity
responds to radios and is indifferent to whether they move. The asymmetry
has been treated throughout the literature as the weakness of each. Read
jointly it is an asset.

cards.back:
It is PROPAGATED, not corrected — it widens the predictive distribution
rather than displacing a point estimate.
cards.front:
What happens to the residual uncertainty in the ratio, and why is that the
right treatment?
cards.title: Propagate, do not correct
cards.why:
So a count that is uncertain because the crowd is unusual is REPORTED as
uncertain. That is behaviour a deployment can act on, and it is behaviour a
scalar correction cannot express. It is also why the output contract had to
be fixed before this chapter: propagation needs somewhere to propagate to.

cards.back:
First, where the joint fit is under-determined the ratio is recoverable
without labels from the deployment's own statistics: stationary devices —
printers, access points, the instrument's own management radios — are
strippable against an empty window. Second, the participant instrument
supplies windows with a KNOWN headcount, making the ratio measured on this
deployment rather than imported.
cards.front:
Name the two fallbacks behind the joint fit, and say why they are stated at
all.
cards.title: The two fallbacks
cards.why:
They are stated because the architecture should not depend on its most
ambitious layer succeeding. This testbed is also better placed than the
office-building precedents for the subtraction, because its empty window is
CERTIFIED rather than presumed.

cards.back:
The transmitter CENSUS recorded with every frame; the DELIVERY DEFICIT of a
paced reference against a same-night control on the other band; and the
ADVERTISEMENT stream. It costs no hardware — all three are already in
every capture the project has taken.
cards.front:
What are the three observables of the device-activity channel, and what
does it cost?
cards.title: The second count channel
cards.why:
Its failure modes are approximately orthogonal to CSI's: CSI counts bodies
through motion and cannot distinguish a still crowd from an empty room,
whereas device activity counts radios and is indifferent to motion.

choices: Into 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz emitters, because only one band carries clients.
Into fleet management radios, infrastructure, and locally-administered addresses — only the third tracks people, and pooling them inflates the count with the instrument's own traffic.
Into strong and weak emitters, since only nearby devices are people.
Into randomised and stable addresses, since only stable ones can be counted reliably.
cards.explanation:
The separation changes the answer entirely. Our own nodes are loud — one
appears as comfortably the loudest emitter in the room. Infrastructure
includes access points advertising several networks from sequential
addresses on one organisational prefix. Only addresses carrying the
locally-administered bit that phones and laptops set when they randomise
track people. Note the inversion in the fourth option: randomised addresses
are the ones that MATTER here, not the ones to discard.
cards.question:
The transmitter census is only meaningful once addresses are separated.
Into what, and why does it change the answer?
cards.title: Three populations, one census

cards.back:
Over more than a thousand minutes of certified-empty observation the
distinct client-address count is ZERO — not small, zero. The control:
infrastructure addresses were captured during EVERY certified-empty hour,
demonstrating the receiver was pulling CSI out of ambient frames throughout
and simply saw no client devices.
cards.front:
State the measured floor of the device-activity channel and the control
that makes it interpretable.
cards.title: The floor, and the control that makes it a measurement
cards.why:
Without that control the zero would be indistinguishable from a dead
receive path. With it, the detection threshold is trivially one randomised
client address — there is no floor to clear.

cards.back:
It is a ONE-CLASS result. There is a rigorous null and NO SENSITIVITY
ESTIMATE whatsoever, so nothing in it speaks to whether the census scales
with the number of people present.
cards.front: The chapter is blunt about the census's limitation. What is it?
cards.title: What the census does NOT establish
cards.why:
The daytime peak observed — a handful of distinct clients — is almost
certainly a single human being: an operator laptop holding sessions to ten
nodes transmits far more than a pocketed phone, and one phone rotating its
address becomes several pseudonyms. The occupancy ramp is designed to
answer exactly this.

choices: Density — BLE is reliable when sparse, CSI at moderate density.
TIME AND OBSERVABILITY — BLE is an intermittent drift-free absolute whose error is a census bias; CSI is a continuous relative whose calibration decays with elapsed time.
Frequency — BLE occupies 2.4 GHz and CSI 5 GHz, so they see different multipath.
Spatial resolution — BLE resolves zones, CSI resolves links.
cards.explanation:
The first option is the RETIRED formulation and it is included because it
was in an earlier draft of this thesis. It was retired for two measured
reasons: the coupled simulation found one modality dominant at EVERY
density while only the staleness switch tracked the error envelope, and the
graded BLE-RSSI density signal the density axis presumed was independently
refuted. The consequence is that the fused estimator is a confidence-weighted
switch on anchor FRESHNESS, not a blend gated on density.
cards.question: On what axis are BLE and CSI complementary?
cards.title: The complementarity axis

cards.back:
In the static-placement regime that proxies a seated crowd — precisely
where the temporal CSI feature collapses toward the fading floor — the BLE
anchor still separates an occupied room from an empty one with a large
effect size, holding up even under substantial simulated advertisement
noise.
cards.front:
A co-registered ray-tracing study gives in-silico support for one half of
the complementarity. Which half, and what does the anchor NOT do?
cards.title: What the co-registered study supports
cards.why:
But its blockage response SATURATES after the first occupants, so in that
layout it resolves occupancy PRESENCE rather than graded headcount. Two
caveats bound it: the BLE measurement noise is a self-authored model, so
this motivates the anchor's role rather than guaranteeing accuracy; and the
penetration-ratio stability the calibration argument rests on is a property
of real device populations.

cards.back:
Nobody measures the FRESHNESS-STRATIFIED error interaction — how the two
modalities' errors relate as a function of how stale the anchor is.
cards.front:
The complementarity claim ends by naming a gap in the whole literature.
What is it?
cards.title: What no published study measures
cards.why:
Establishing it on hardware is the drift-study leg of the pre-registered
campaign. A claim that identifies a gap AND owns the instrument that could
close it is in a much stronger position than one that merely notes an
absence.

cards.back:
BLE RSSI noise propagates through the per-environment path-loss model to a
per-device distance variance, which maps to a count-domain standard
deviation via the occupancy model's Jacobian. τ is a chosen multiple of
that propagated uncertainty.
cards.front: How is the recalibration threshold τ derived, rather than tuned?
cards.title: The trigger threshold
cards.why:
So only drift exceeding the NOISE FLOOR OF THE REFERENCE ITSELF fires a
campaign. A threshold picked by hand would be arbitrary; a threshold
derived from the reference's own noise is defensible in one sentence. A
hysteresis condition — exceedance persisting across two consecutive
campaigns — bounds the false-trigger rate on top.

cards.back:
The per-subcarrier complex channel frequency response a commodity OFDM
receiver estimates during demodulation. Under the narrowband model
Y(k) = H(k)X(k) + N(k), CSI is the vector of recovered H(k) over the
occupied subcarriers. In MIMO it becomes a tensor indexed by
transmit–receive antenna pair, each entry decomposing into an amplitude and
a phase.
cards.front: Define CSI precisely enough that a sceptic cannot accuse you of hand-waving.
cards.title: What CSI is
cards.why:
Two consequences follow immediately: the channel is sampled at subcarrier
